notes: Youth arson sentencing appeal; Hallett J's welfare analysis of section 91 detention is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: R v R and L: youth arson sentencing and section 91 detention
key_facts: Two boys aged 12 and 13 pleaded guilty to arson being reckless as to whether life was endangered after repeatedly trying to set fire to a drunk man on CCTV in Ramsgate.
R had an extensive record and was in secure accommodation; L was of previous good character but emotionally vulnerable and under the influence of drugs and alcohol.
The Crown Court imposed section 91 detention of three years on R and two years on L after a group attack that burnt a hole in the victim's clothing.
Both appealed, arguing the sentences were excessive and that L should not have received custody.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the Single Judge against section 91 detention sentences imposed in the Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; substantial detention was inevitable given the gravity of the offence and the boys' need for stability, structure and secure accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: For grave arson endangering life by very young offenders, substantial section 91 detention may be appropriate where secure accommodation provides necessary stability and protection even if the welfare of the child and public protection pull in the same direction.
legal_issues: Whether section 91 detention was excessive for children aged 12 and 13 on guilty pleas
Whether L's sentence was wrong in principle given pre-sentence report recommendations
How welfare considerations and public protection interact in youth sentencing
Appropriate starting point compared with an adult sentence

confidence.notes: Facts, sentencing reasoning and dismissal of both appeals are clearly recorded.

notes: Stay of execution application; Thomas LJ applies CPR Part 52.7 principles and criticises costs conduct.

enrichment.short_title: Haydock Finance v Louis Transport: stay of execution and indemnity costs
key_facts: Haydock Finance obtained a Birmingham County Court judgment for about £34,000 against Louis Transport Equipment Consultants and related defendants.
The defendants sought a stay pending appeal after leave was granted, having declined an offer to pay into the claimant's solicitor account.
A sheriff levied execution by walking possession before the stay application was determined.
The oral stay hearing incurred disproportionate costs relative to the sum in issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal for a stay of execution pending appeal from a county court money judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Stay application dismissed; claimant entitled to enforce; oral hearing costs ordered to lie where they fall; indemnity costs ordered for the failed stay application; sheriff's levy held justified.
enrichment.ratio: Absent inability to pay or risk of irrecoverability, there are no grounds for a stay of execution merely because an appeal is listed within two months; a successful judgment creditor may enforce immediately and a doomed stay application may attract indemnity costs.
legal_issues: Whether a stay of execution should be granted pending appeal under CPR Part 52.7
Whether the claimant was entitled to instruct the sheriff before the stay hearing
Allocation of costs where the application should have been dealt with on paper
Whether indemnity costs were appropriate for a hopeless stay application

Hammond Suddards Solicitors v Agrichem International Holding Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 2065

notes: Permission refused in police malicious prosecution action; Castorina and Perks principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Khadine v Commissioner of Police: permission refused on wrongful arrest appeal
key_facts: Mr Khadine, a mini-cab driver, claimed unlawful arrest, malicious prosecution, misfeasance, negligence and racial discrimination after a fare dispute with two women in Croydon.
Police cross-reports led to his arrest and charge for assault despite his own complaint; the CPS later discontinued proceedings.
Grigson J discharged the jury and entered judgment for the Commissioner, holding no jury issue on honest belief or reasonable cause.
The litigant in person sought permission to appeal, relying on alleged police bias and procedural unfairness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal an order entering judgment for the police after discharge of the jury in a civil claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no realistic prospect of overturning the judge's ruling that DC Aspinall had reasonable grounds to arrest and that disputed factual challenges did not require jury questions on dishonesty.
enrichment.ratio: Where objective grounds for arrest and prosecution exist, a judge may properly withhold from the jury questions of an officer's actual belief unless cogent evidence of dishonesty exists; mere challenge in cross-examination does not create a conflict of evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the judge usurped the jury's function on unlawful arrest and malicious prosecution
Application of Castorina and Perks on when honesty questions go to the jury
Whether exclusion of Collins J's judicial review observations was lawful
Whether Article 6 required trial of disputed police conduct

notes: Planning section 288 challenge; Evans-Lombe J distinguishes Thurrock on dwelling-house use immunity.

enrichment.short_title: Swale BC v Lee: lawful residential use of barn and section 171B immunity
key_facts: Roger Lee occupied a converted barn at Newnham using incorporated mobile homes as a dwelling after successive planning appeals and quashed inspector decisions.
Swale Borough Council challenged a third inspector's grant of a certificate of lawfulness, quashing of an enforcement notice and unconditional planning permission.
The inspector found continuous residential use as a single dwelling house for more than four years before the LDC application despite intermittent occupation.
The council argued the inspector wrongly applied abandonment and dormancy reasoning rejected in Thurrock.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application and related section 289 appeal to quash an inspector's decision on a certificate of lawfulness of existing use.
enrichment.outcome: Application failed; the inspector's four-year residential use finding was not Wednesbury unreasonable and his reasoning on temporary absence from a dwelling differed materially from the airfield use in Thurrock.
enrichment.ratio: Temporary non-occupation of a building used as a dwelling does not necessarily break residential use for section 171B purposes; intention not to abandon and improvement works may support continuity, unlike cessation of an active airfield use.
legal_issues: Whether the barn had been used as a single dwelling house for four years
Whether the inspector erred by relying on absence of abandonment or future intention
Application of Thurrock Borough Council v Secretary of State to dwelling use
Whether failure to explain departure from earlier inspectors vitiated the decision

Edwards v Bairstow [1956] AC 14

notes: Landmark local plan judicial review; Collins J quashes Wealden's abandonment of statutory plan process.

enrichment.short_title: Martin Grant Homes v Wealden: unlawful abandonment of emerging local plan
key_facts: Wealden District Council abandoned its statutory local plan review and proposed adopting a non-statutory draft plan while commencing a Local Development Framework after GOSE pressure.
Developers Martin Grant Homes challenged the decision after their Uckfield housing site was removed from the first deposit draft local plan.
The 2004 Act transitional provisions required authorities with unresolved objections to continue the 1990 Act local plan process.
The council cited cost savings, housing delivery and Planning Delivery Grant concerns in deciding not to hold a public inquiry.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim to quash the council's decision to discontinue the statutory local plan review process.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; decision to abandon the statutory local plan process quashed; council required to continue the 1990 Act procedure including republication under section 40(2) and a local inquiry.
enrichment.ratio: Parliament's Schedule 8 transitional arrangements must be followed where an emerging local plan had reached first deposit with unresolved objections; economic convenience or GOSE pressure is not an exceptional reason to abandon the statutory process under Persimmon principles.
legal_issues: Whether the council lawfully abandoned the statutory local plan review
Construction of Schedule 8 paragraphs 8 to 10 of the 2004 Act
Scope of the power in Persimmon Homes v North Hertfordshire to withdraw an emerging plan
Effect of GOSE letters and Planning Delivery Grant considerations on the decision

enrichment.short_title: ID v Home Office: costs order after immigration detention appeal
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal's main judgment in the Roma family's immigration detention litigation, the court considered costs of the appeal.
The appellants had substantially succeeded on the principal issue concerning false imprisonment and officer immunity.
The Home Office had lost on some points but benefited from the court's reasoning on remaining issues.
Brooke LJ declined to reduce the appellants' costs award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental Court of Appeal hearing on costs after the principal judgment in an immigration detention appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appellants awarded costs here and below in full without deduction despite partial losses on subsidiary issues.
enrichment.ratio: Where appellants essentially win the main issue on appeal, a costs deduction is not appropriate merely because they lost on lesser points that still produced useful guidance for the Home Office.
legal_issues: Whether costs should be reduced where an appellant succeeds on the main issue but loses on others
Appropriate costs consequence after a partially successful public law appeal

notes: Urgent judicial review of youth court detention; Moses J quashes sentence and substitutes conditional discharge.

enrichment.short_title: K v Croydon Crown Court: Ethiopian asylum seeker youth sentence quashed
key_facts: A 17-year-old Ethiopian asylum seeker was convicted of seeking leave to enter by deception after denying a prior entry clearance application made under an agent's false name.
The Bromley Youth Court and Croydon Crown Court imposed a four-month detention and training order despite positive pre-sentence reports and no prior offending.
She had been screened without a responsible adult present and said the agent instructed her to conceal the earlier application.
Judicial review was brought urgently while she remained in custody.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for judicial review, granted permission and determined substantively, of a Crown Court appeal upholding a youth court sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Sentence quashed as wrong in law; substituted with a twelve-month conditional discharge because the influence of the agent and lack of responsible adult screening were not properly considered.
enrichment.ratio: Ignoring the powerful influence of immigration agents on vulnerable minors, especially where screening guidance requiring a responsible adult was breached, may render a custodial sentence wrong in law even where the offence is established.
legal_issues: Whether custody was the only appropriate sentence for a first-time 17-year-old offender
Relevance of agent influence and Article 31 Refugee Convention context
Whether the Crown Court erred in treating custody as the entry point
Scope of judicial review of youth court sentencing rather than Court of Appeal review

notes: Chancery appeal on Part 36 costs consequences; Lightman J upholds indemnity costs for defective offer.

enrichment.short_title: Hertsmere PCT v Balasubramanian estate: Part 36 costs and overriding objective
key_facts: Primary care trusts claimed repayment of about £390,000 in fraudulent optician sight-test overpayments from the estate of Dr Balasubramanian after his death stopped prosecution.
The Court of Appeal had already granted summary judgment for an account; Master Bowman assessed overpayments and applied CPR Part 36.21 after a better-than-offer judgment.
The claimants' July 2003 settlement offer omitted the required Part 36.5 wording on acceptance after 21 days.
The estate's solicitors deliberately withheld identification of the non-compliance until the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's order awarding enhanced interest and indemnity costs under CPR Part 36.21 after account judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; master rightly ordered indemnity costs and 10% above base rate interest despite technical non-compliance, and permission to appeal the account judgment was refused.
enrichment.ratio: A materially defective Part 36 offer may still attract Part 36.21 consequences where the defect is obvious and the offeree deliberately withholds it in breach of the overriding objective to cooperate and save expense.
legal_issues: Whether CPR Part 36.21 applied to a non-compliant settlement offer
Whether it was unjust to order indemnity costs and enhanced interest
Whether the estate's failure to identify non-compliance should be taken into account
Whether permission to appeal the account judgment should be granted
linked_authorities: Mitchell v James [2002] EWCA Civ 997

notes: Cross-border insolvency freezing-order appeals; Mance LJ on jurisdiction and Mareva limits.

enrichment.short_title: Fourie v Le Roux: cross-border freezing orders and insolvency jurisdiction
key_facts: South African provisional liquidator Mr Fourie obtained English freezing orders against Mr Le Roux and Fintrade over alleged stripping of assets from alloy-wheel companies HEE and HEI.
Park J granted a £3.4m Mareva injunction on a section 426 letter of request, later discharged by Jarvis QC for want of jurisdiction.
Further freezing orders were granted against HEE on English causes of action; Blackburne J capped them at £750,000, later increased to £900,000 on appeal.
Le Roux claimed credit for paying HEE's Wesbank, Cutfin and Bankfin debts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals concerning jurisdiction, quantum and costs of successive freezing orders in cross-border insolvency proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: First appeal largely dismissed but costs apportioned; second appeal on quantum dismissed; HEE's cross-appeal allowed in part to increase the freezing limit to £900,000 including £150,000 for costs.
enrichment.ratio: A freezing order requires activated jurisdiction through substantive English proceedings or a valid foreign-proceedings basis under section 25; section 426 and an insufficient letter of request cannot alone support Mareva relief, though English claims by the company may justify a properly quantified order.
legal_issues: Whether section 426 or section 25 CJJA supported the first freezing order
Whether causes of action existed before interim relief was granted
Whether cross-claims for debt payments should reduce the Mareva limit
Whether legal costs should be included in a freezing order cap

notes: Guarantee waiver appeal; Court of Appeal applies Misrepresentation Act section 2(2) to refuse rescission.

enrichment.short_title: UCB v Thomason: guarantee waiver, misrepresentation and section 2(2)
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Thomason gave guarantees exceeding £2.9 million for a failed nursing-home company and negotiated a January 1997 waiver accepting about £34,000 from a family loan.
They swore affidavits of affairs containing misleading statements about the Bromsgrove home, Carysfort Road sale and related family trusts and companies.
Pumfrey J found non-fraudulent misrepresentation but refused rescission under section 2(2) because no better recovery was shown than the waiver payment.
The bank appealed seeking enforcement of the guarantees or rescission of the waiver.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery trial judgment dismissing a bank's claim to revive guarantee liability after a waiver agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; waiver construction limited rescission to discovery of further assets; section 2(2) made it inequitable to rescind where the bank's lost chance of greater recovery was not established.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 2(2) of the Misrepresentation Act, rescission of a performed compromise may be refused where the misrepresentation caused no significant financial loss measured by the lost chance of a better settlement or bankruptcy dividend, even if the misrepresentation was intentional and fundamental.
legal_issues: Construction of the waiver's 'on the basis that' full disclosure clause
Whether non-disclosure entitled the bank to treat the waiver as at an end
Assessment of loss for section 2(2) where guarantees were largely unrecoverable
Whether rescission should be ordered for intentional non-fraudulent misrepresentation
